_meta.description: Curated micro-lesson / technique topic allowlist for slideshow posts, split about evenly between upper high school and younger high school (ages 13–15). Stage 1 (assign.py) rotates through this list; Stage 2 is NOT allowed to write about anything outside it. The bot may propose additions -- a human approves them before they're added here.
selection_rules: Stable, well-established material only -- nothing at the edge of active scientific/scholarly dispute.

Nothing where curricula meaningfully disagree on the substance or the 'right' framing -- a real hazard across the product's actual curriculum list (IB MYP/DP, AP, AQA, CBSE, CXC, Edexcel, French Bac, German Abitur, ICSE, NSW HSC, Cambridge IGCSE, VCE, WJEC). safe_for below is deliberately conservative.
Nothing that needs a diagram to teach -- slideshows explicitly carry no diagrams or graphs (a wrong diagram is confidently wrong and slips past review because it looks like a diagram).
No live policy/political framing -- economics and psychology entries stick to mechanism and definition, not current-events application.

safe_for 'all' means genuinely curriculum-agnostic (a physical law, a mathematical identity, a definitional concept taught the same way everywhere); anything narrower says which boards it's been checked against.
archetype is 'micro-lesson' for curriculum content, 'technique' for study-skills content that isn't tied to any subject.

Nothing sensitive for a 13-18 audience: no reproduction or sexual-health content, drugs, gambling or betting framing, mental-health diagnoses, or anything that reads as personal medical or health advice. Biology and psychology entries stay at the level of mechanism.

Psychology and learning-science entries rely only on findings that have held up under replication. Don't build a deck on the Stanford prison experiment, ego depletion, power posing, the laptop-vs-longhand note-taking study, or a precise '7 plus or minus 2' memory span -- and 'learning styles' appears only as a myth-busting deck.

No near-duplicates: every entry should produce a deck that couldn't be mistaken for another entry's. Related entries are fine (their notes say how they differ) as long as the core lesson is different.

Micro-lessons are split about evenly between upper high school (AP, IB DP, A-Level, grades 11–12) and younger high school (ages 13–15: US grades 8–10, GCSE/IGCSE Years 9–11, IB MYP 3–5, CBSE/ICSE classes 8–10). Nothing is aimed below 13. Each entry has level "upper", "younger", or "both" -- technique entries are "both" because the same study skill suits either age. Where a subject is taught at both ages, the two levels stay roughly even. Economics and psychology stay upper because those courses start later. A younger entry that simplifies an upper one says in its notes how the two differ.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.topic: Le Chatelier's principle
topics.notes: Already built as the first example deck (post-templates/slideshow/output/lechatelier-principle/). Equilibrium shift direction is universal chemistry, no diagram needed -- describable via the equilibrium expression and qualitative shift rules. A separate younger deck only defines what a reversible reaction is; this one is the shift rules.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.topic: Strong vs. weak acids and bases
topics.notes: Strong acids and bases dissociate completely in water; weak ones only partly. That's the distinction every board shares. Don't adjudicate Arrhenius vs. Brønsted-Lowry definitions, and don't drift into pH-calculation edge cases that vary by syllabus depth. The younger deck on reactions only does the word equation for neutralisation.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.topic: Oxidation states and redox reactions
topics.notes: Electron-transfer framing is universal: oxidation is loss of electrons, reduction is gain. Give both common mnemonics (OIL RIG in the UK, LEO the lion says GER in the US) or neither. Stick to identifying oxidation/reduction, not balancing complex half-equations, which varies by board depth.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.topic: Breaking bonds takes energy -- it doesn't release it
topics.notes: Top-tier misconception, universal: breaking bonds is always endothermic and making them exothermic; the overall sign depends on the balance. Stay qualitative -- bond-enthalpy data varies between boards' data booklets.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.topic: What a catalyst does (and doesn't) change
topics.notes: Universal: a catalyst provides a pathway with lower activation energy and speeds up forward and reverse reactions alike, so it changes neither the equilibrium position nor the enthalpy change. The Maxwell-Boltzmann explanation is a graph -- leave it out. What makes collisions successful (concentration, temperature, surface area) is the younger collision-theory deck.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.topic: Dynamic equilibrium doesn't mean equal amounts
topics.notes: Common misconception, universal: at equilibrium the forward and reverse RATES are equal, not the concentrations. Different from the existing Le Chatelier deck (that's about shifts; this is about what equilibrium is). The younger reversible-reaction deck stops at the definition and does not say what equilibrium is.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.topic: Boiling water doesn't break any water molecules
topics.notes: Universal, and only about what breaks: boiling overcomes the forces between molecules, not the covalent bonds inside them -- steam is still water molecules. Names for intermolecular forces vary by board (London/dispersion, van der Waals, induced dipole-dipole), so say 'intermolecular forces' and don't commit to one scheme. Why the temperature holds steady is the latent-heat deck. The younger states-of-matter deck stops at particles moving further apart and never mentions bonds.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.topic: Why ice floats
topics.notes: Hydrogen bonding holds ice in an open arrangement, so solid water is less dense than liquid -- unusual among substances, and universal. Bonus fact: liquid water is densest around 4 °C. Describe the structure in words; no lattice diagram.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.topic: pH is logarithmic: pH 3 is ten times more acidic than pH 4
topics.notes: Universal: each pH unit is a factor of 10 in hydrogen-ion concentration. Different from the existing strong-vs-weak-acids deck. Avoid pH values of specific products (they vary); pure water at pH 7 (at 25 °C) is safe.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.topic: Like dissolves like: why oil and water don't mix
topics.notes: Polarity-based solubility, universal at this level. Keep it qualitative (polar with polar, non-polar with non-polar); skip the thermodynamics of dissolving.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.topic: Where does the mass go when wood burns?
topics.notes: Conservation of mass, universal: the 'missing' mass leaves as gases (carbon dioxide and water vapour); in a closed system the total is unchanged. Keep combustion equations simple and balanced.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.topic: Collision theory: what actually speeds up a reaction
topics.notes: Universal: rate depends on how often particles collide with at least the activation energy. Cover concentration, temperature, and surface area in words. Leave catalysts to their own deck so the two don't overlap. At 13–15 stay qualitative: concentration, temperature, and surface area only. No rate equations and no distribution curve. Catalysts are a separate, older deck.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.topic: Isotopes: same element, different mass
topics.notes: Definitional and universal (same number of protons, different neutrons, same chemical behaviour). Carbon-12 vs. carbon-14 is the clean example; relative atomic mass as a weighted average is a fine extension. At 13–15, stop at same protons, different neutrons, and carbon-12 vs. carbon-14. Leave the weighted-average relative-atomic-mass calculation out.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.topic: Why salt conducts when dissolved but not as a solid
topics.notes: Universal: ions have to be free to move. Covers ionic structure without a lattice diagram. Stay on ionic compounds only -- whether bonding is taught as an ionic/covalent spectrum varies by board.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.topic: Metallic bonding: why metals conduct
topics.notes: The positive-ions-in-a-sea-of-delocalised-electrons model is taught everywhere at this level. Cover conductivity and malleability in words; no structure diagram.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.topic: Diamond vs. graphite: same atoms, different properties
topics.notes: Allotropes of carbon, universal. Explain hardness and conductivity from bonding in words (four bonds each vs. three plus delocalised electrons between layers). No structure diagrams.

topics.subject: Biology
topics.topic: Natural selection vs. genetic drift
topics.notes: Foundational, non-controversial evolutionary biology distinction (selection vs. random allele-frequency change, strongest in small populations). Upper-level only: younger courses teach natural selection but usually not genetic drift.

topics.subject: Biology
topics.topic: Dominant doesn't mean common
topics.notes: Classic genetics misconception, universal: dominance is about how two alleles interact in one organism, not how frequent an allele is in a population. Use Mendel's peas or a hypothetical trait -- avoid human disease or appearance examples that could feel personal.

topics.subject: Biology
topics.topic: Genes, alleles, genotype, phenotype: the vocabulary untangled
topics.notes: Definitional and universal. Mendel's pea plants (flower colour) make a neutral running example taught everywhere. Leave Punnett squares out -- the definitions don't need them.

topics.subject: Biology
topics.topic: Mitosis vs. meiosis: what each one is for
topics.notes: Purpose-level comparison (genetically identical cells for growth and repair vs. genetically varied gametes with half the chromosomes) is universal. Don't walk through phases -- stage detail varies by board and depends on diagrams. Keep reproduction strictly at the cell level.

topics.subject: Biology
topics.topic: From DNA to protein in two steps
topics.notes: Transcription and translation (DNA to mRNA to protein) at the depth every board teaches. Avoid deeper molecular detail (splicing, named enzymes) that some syllabi include and others don't.

topics.subject: Biology
topics.topic: Why cells are so small: surface area to volume
topics.notes: Universal: volume grows faster than surface area, so a big cell can't exchange materials fast enough. The 1 cm vs. 2 cm cube calculation fits in math blocks -- numbers, not a diagram.

topics.subject: Biology
topics.topic: Homeostasis: how your body holds its temperature steady
topics.notes: Negative feedback, universal. Temperature control (sweating, shivering, changes in skin blood flow) is the standard example. Avoid blood-glucose/diabetes framing, which edges into health conditions.

topics.subject: Biology
topics.topic: Nerves vs. hormones: two ways your body sends messages
topics.notes: Universal comparison (fast, short-lived, targeted vs. slower, longer-lasting, widespread). Adrenaline is a safe hormone example; keep reproductive hormones out entirely.

topics.subject: Biology
topics.topic: Mutations aren't always harmful
topics.notes: Universal: most mutations are neutral, some harmful, a few beneficial -- and they're the raw material of variation. Use non-human examples (antibiotic resistance as a benefit to the bacterium); avoid human genetic disease. Why antibiotics don't work on viruses is a separate deck. Here, antibiotic resistance is only the example of a mutation that helps the bacterium.

topics.subject: Biology
topics.topic: Immune memory: why the second infection is milder
topics.notes: Memory cells and the faster, larger secondary response are universal textbook content. Naming vaccination as the application is fine, but mechanism only -- no vaccine policy, safety debates, or health advice.

topics.subject: Biology
topics.topic: Osmosis vs. diffusion
topics.notes: Classic intro-biology distinction, no diagram required. Courses phrase osmosis differently (dilute to concentrated solution, high to low water concentration, or water potential at upper levels), so say it plainly: water moves across a partially permeable membrane from where there's more water to where there's less. Don't commit to any one board's term.

topics.subject: Biology
topics.topic: Prokaryotes vs. eukaryotes
topics.notes: Definitional and universal (no nucleus or membrane-bound organelles vs. both present). Don't imply prokaryotic DNA is unorganised -- it sits in a nucleoid, often with plasmids. Endosymbiosis gets a mention at most.

topics.subject: Biology
topics.topic: Arteries vs. veins: it's direction, not oxygen
topics.notes: Universal definition: arteries carry blood away from the heart, veins towards it. The pulmonary artery (carrying deoxygenated blood) is the famous exception to the 'arteries carry oxygen-rich blood' rule of thumb -- that's the hook. Words only, no heart diagram.

topics.subject: Biology
topics.topic: Enzymes don't die -- they denature
topics.notes: Universal: heat or the wrong pH changes the active site's shape so the substrate no longer fits. Don't pick between lock-and-key and induced-fit (boards teach them at different depths) -- just describe the shape change. Enzymes aren't alive, which is the hook. Which digestive organ does which job is a different deck. Here, only what denature means.

topics.subject: Biology
topics.topic: Why plants are green
topics.notes: Universal: chlorophyll absorbs mostly red and blue light and reflects green. Hook: plants reject the colour they're famous for. No absorption-spectrum graph. Only the colour. Where a plant's mass comes from is a different deck.

topics.subject: Biology
topics.topic: Where a tree's mass actually comes from
topics.notes: Mostly from carbon dioxide in the air, via photosynthesis -- not from the soil. Universal and strongly counterintuitive. Van Helmont's willow experiment is the historical angle (he concluded water, which was only part of the story). Keep the photosynthesis equation simple, typeset with mhchem. Don't explain why leaves look green; that's a different deck.

topics.subject: Biology
topics.topic: Why antibiotics don't work on viruses
topics.notes: Universal: antibiotics target structures and processes bacteria have and viruses don't. Strictly educational -- no medical advice, no 'what to take when you're ill', no fear framing about resistance.

topics.subject: Biology
topics.topic: Why food chains are short
topics.notes: Universal: energy is lost at each step (movement, heat, waste). The '10%' figure is a rough rule of thumb that varies a lot between ecosystems -- present it as approximate. Describe the chain in words, no pyramid diagram. How several chains link into a food web is a different deck. Here, only why a single chain can't be long.

topics.subject: Physics
topics.topic: Why a satellite in orbit isn't 'zero gravity'
topics.notes: Free-fall framing of orbits is standard physics, addresses a widespread misconception, explainable purely verbally/algebraically.

topics.subject: Physics
topics.topic: Conservation of momentum in collisions
topics.notes: Core mechanics, universal across boards. Stick to the principle and elastic-vs-inelastic definitions, not diagram-dependent vector problems.

topics.subject: Physics
topics.topic: Holding a heavy box does zero work on it
topics.notes: Physics 'work' (force x distance moved in the direction of the force) vs. everyday effort -- universal, counterintuitive hook. Be precise: your muscles still use energy internally; it's no work done ON THE BOX.

topics.subject: Physics
topics.topic: Double the speed, four times the braking distance
topics.notes: KE = 1/2 mv^2 is universal; with the same braking force, braking distance scales with v^2 because the brakes must remove four times the energy. Keep it to the physics -- no road-safety lecture, no country-specific stopping-distance tables.

topics.subject: Physics
topics.topic: How airbags work: stretching out the stopping time
topics.notes: F = change in momentum / time, universal: the same momentum change over a longer time means a smaller force. Different lesson from the existing conservation-of-momentum deck (force and time, not collisions). Mechanism only -- no crash statistics.

topics.subject: Physics
topics.topic: Latent heat: why melting ice stays at 0 °C
topics.notes: Universal, and only about the temperature plateau: while ice melts or water boils, the energy supplied goes into the change of state, so the temperature stays put until it's done. Stay qualitative; specific-latent-heat symbols vary by board. What does and doesn't break when water boils is the boiling deck -- don't restate it.

topics.subject: Physics
topics.topic: The Doppler effect
topics.notes: Universal: waves bunch up ahead of a moving source (higher pitch) and stretch out behind it (lower pitch). A passing siren is the canonical example. Stay qualitative -- the equations differ in form and depth across boards.

topics.subject: Physics
topics.topic: Half-life: random for one atom, predictable for billions
topics.notes: Universal. Individual decays are random; a large sample halves in a fixed time. Coin or dice analogies work. No health or radiation-dose claims. How geologists use that decay to date a rock, as opposed to putting layers in order, is the Earth-science dating deck.

topics.subject: Physics
topics.topic: Nuclear fission vs. fusion
topics.notes: Definitional and universal (splitting heavy nuclei vs. joining light ones; the Sun runs on fusion). Mechanism only -- no nuclear-power policy or weapons framing.

topics.subject: Physics
topics.topic: Why the sky is blue
topics.notes: Rayleigh scattering (shorter wavelengths scatter more) is settled physics, even though not every syllabus covers it. Also explains red sunsets (a longer path through air). If 'why not violet?' comes up, keep the answer brief (the Sun's spectrum plus how our eyes respond). Mention the 'it reflects the ocean' myth only to debunk it.

topics.subject: Physics
topics.topic: Centripetal force isn't a new kind of force
topics.notes: Universal: 'centripetal' names a direction (towards the centre), and an existing force does the job (tension, gravity, friction). Also covers why constant-speed circular motion is still acceleration. On 'centrifugal force', say only that it isn't a real outward force acting on the object -- don't get into reference frames.

topics.subject: Physics
topics.topic: Power vs. energy: what an electricity bill actually charges for
topics.notes: Universal: power is the rate of energy transfer; the kilowatt-hour is a unit of energy. Keep the bill framing generic -- no real tariffs, prices, or country-specific figures.

topics.subject: Physics
topics.topic: Why a steel ship floats
topics.notes: Archimedes' principle and average density, universal. A solid steel block sinks; a hollow hull displaces enough water to support its weight. Salinity and temperature effects on water density get a passing mention at most. Pressure (force over area) is a separate, younger deck.

topics.subject: Physics
topics.topic: Mass vs. weight
topics.notes: Universal: mass (kg) is the amount of matter; weight is a force (N), W = mg. The hook: your mass is the same on the Moon, your weight isn't. Use g = 9.8 N/kg (some courses use 9.81, some round to 10) and say so once.

topics.subject: Physics
topics.topic: Newton's first law: things don't need a force to keep moving
topics.notes: Targets the deep-rooted 'motion needs a push' misconception; universal. Explain why everyday objects slow down (friction and air resistance are forces). Different law and misconception from the existing Newton's-third-law deck.

topics.subject: Physics
topics.topic: Newton's third law, correctly stated
topics.notes: Targets the most common misconception (forces act on DIFFERENT objects, so they never cancel) -- a classic 'sounds obvious, is usually misunderstood' micro-lesson. Universal, no diagram needed.

topics.subject: Physics
topics.topic: Why heavy and light objects fall at the same rate
topics.notes: Universal: with negligible air resistance, everything falls with the same acceleration; air resistance explains the everyday exceptions. The Galileo leaning-tower story is historically doubtful -- use Apollo 15's hammer-and-feather drop on the Moon (1971), which actually happened.

topics.subject: Physics
topics.topic: Energy isn't used up, it's transferred
topics.notes: Conservation of energy, universal. Vocabulary differs by board ('energy stores and pathways' vs. 'forms of energy'), so describe transfers plainly without committing to either framework's labels.

topics.subject: Physics
topics.topic: Heat vs. temperature
topics.notes: Universal distinction (temperature relates to the average kinetic energy of particles; heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference). A bath vs. a cup of boiling water is the classic contrast. Keep definitions at the level every board shares. Why metal feels colder than wood at the same temperature is conductivity, covered in its own deck.

topics.subject: Physics
topics.topic: Why metal feels colder than wood at the same temperature
topics.notes: Thermal conductivity, universal, excellent hook: both are at room temperature, but metal conducts heat away from your hand faster. No diagram needed. Heat vs. temperature (what the two words mean) is a separate deck; this one is which material conducts heat away faster.

topics.subject: Physics
topics.topic: Pressure: why a sharp knife cuts and snowshoes don't sink
topics.notes: P = F / A, universal. Two everyday examples pulling in opposite directions carry the whole lesson. Why a hollow steel ship floats is average density and displaced water, not this deck.

topics.subject: Physics
topics.topic: Why there's no sound in space
topics.notes: Sound is a mechanical wave that needs particles; light doesn't. Universal. Sci-fi explosions are the hook -- keep it light and don't dunk on a specific film.

topics.subject: Physics
topics.topic: Current isn't used up in a circuit
topics.notes: Universal misconception-correction: current is the same all the way round a single loop; energy is what gets transferred to components. One simple loop described in words -- anything needing a circuit diagram is out. Series vs. parallel is a separate deck; this one is a single loop.

topics.subject: Physics
topics.topic: Friction: the force that lets you walk
topics.notes: Counterintuitive and universal: static friction pushes you forward when your foot pushes back on the ground. Links to Newton's third law but is its own lesson. Keep static vs. kinetic friction qualitative. Newton's third law (forces come in pairs on different objects) is its own deck; use the pair here only to explain the step.

topics.subject: Earth science
topics.topic: Why Earth has seasons (it's not distance from the Sun)
topics.notes: Classic misconception; the universal answer is axial tilt (the angle of sunlight and day length). The killer fact: Earth is closest to the Sun in early January, during northern-hemisphere winter. Explainable without a diagram. This deck is only why seasons happen. Weather vs. climate is the definition of those two words, and day-to-day weather is not this lesson.

topics.subject: Science skills
topics.topic: Random vs. systematic error
topics.notes: Universal: repeating measurements reduces the effect of random error but does nothing for systematic error (e.g. a balance that isn't zeroed). Connects to the accuracy-vs-precision deck but shouldn't restate it.

topics.subject: Science skills
topics.topic: Reliability vs. validity
topics.notes: Research-methods terms, psychology-style: reliability is getting consistent results; validity is measuring what you meant to measure. Example: a 'reading test' that only times how fast students read gives the same scores every week (reliable) but doesn't measure understanding (not valid). Don't use measuring-instrument errors -- that's the random-vs-systematic-error and accuracy-vs-precision decks. Note that some school science courses use 'valid' more loosely (a fair test that answers the question); say so once.

topics.subject: Science skills
topics.topic: Clever Hans: why good experiments are double-blind
topics.notes: The well-documented story of a horse that seemed to do arithmetic but was reading unconscious cues from its questioners -- a great hook for experimenter bias and why double-blind design hides the condition from researchers as well as participants. Keep the focus on the researchers' side; don't build the deck around placebo effects.

topics.subject: Science skills
topics.topic: Independent, dependent, and control variables
topics.notes: Universal across every science course. One invented experiment (how water temperature affects how long sugar takes to dissolve) labels all three. Boards say 'control variable' or 'controlled variable' -- use both once.

topics.subject: Science skills
topics.topic: Accuracy vs. precision
topics.notes: Universal measurement distinction. The dartboard analogy is usually a picture -- describe it in words. Stick to the shared core definitions; finer measurement vocabulary varies by board.

topics.subject: Science skills
topics.topic: Significant figures: why 2.0 isn't the same as 2
topics.notes: Universal idea: trailing zeros communicate how precisely something was measured. Edge-case rules vary slightly between boards -- stick to the core rules and the why.

topics.subject: Math
topics.topic: What a derivative actually measures (instantaneous rate of change)
topics.notes: Conceptual (not mechanical/procedural) framing avoids notation differences across boards (Leibniz vs. Lagrange) -- keep it to the idea, not a worked differentiation example.

topics.subject: Math
topics.topic: What a logarithm is actually asking
topics.notes: Frame log_b(x) as 'what power of b gives x?' -- the inverse of exponentiation. Universal. Stick to the definition and a couple of clean examples; notation conventions differ (log vs. lg vs. ln), so define whichever one the deck uses.

topics.subject: Math
topics.topic: Permutations vs. combinations: when order matters
topics.notes: Universal counting principle. One everyday example of each (a race podium vs. choosing a team) carries it. nPr/nCr notation varies across boards and calculators -- describe the idea and use factorial formulas rather than leaning on one notation.

topics.subject: Math
topics.topic: The birthday problem: why 23 people is enough
topics.notes: Classic, undisputed probability result (just over a 50% chance that two of 23 people share a birthday). State the assumptions (365 equally likely days, ignore leap years). The real lesson is the complement trick -- work out the chance that nobody shares.

topics.subject: Math
topics.topic: False positives and the base-rate trap
topics.notes: Conditional probability with a strong hook: a '99% accurate' test for something rare still produces mostly false positives. Use a clearly hypothetical scenario with round numbers -- never a real disease, real test, or anything that reads as medical advice.

topics.subject: Math
topics.topic: Why √2 is irrational (proof by contradiction)
topics.notes: Classic proof, identical everywhere it's taught, and a clean first look at proof by contradiction. Walk the standard even/even argument in short math-block steps -- it suits the slide format because each step is small.

topics.subject: Math
topics.topic: Where the quadratic formula comes from
topics.notes: Pure algebra, universal: derive it by completing the square on ax^2 + bx + c = 0. The payoff is never having to memorise it blind again. Keep each slide to one or two algebra steps so nothing overflows.

topics.subject: Math
topics.topic: The chain rule, as rates multiplying
topics.notes: Conceptual framing (if y changes 3 times as fast as u, and u changes 2 times as fast as x, then y changes 6 times as fast as x) is universal. Show dy/dx = (dy/du)(du/dx) once; no pile of worked differentiation. Assumes the reader knows what a derivative is -- the existing derivative-rate-of-change deck covers that.

topics.subject: Math
topics.topic: The fundamental theorem of calculus, in plain words
topics.notes: Differentiation and integration as inverse processes -- universal wherever calculus is taught. Keep it verbal and algebraic (accumulated change vs. rate of change). Naming 'area under a curve' is fine, but don't lean on a graph the deck can't show.

topics.subject: Math
topics.topic: Why e^x is its own derivative
topics.notes: Universal. Frame e as the base whose growth rate equals its current value; the continuous-compounding limit is a fine way in, framed as maths rather than money advice. No rigorous limit proof -- why it matters is the lesson.

topics.subject: Math
topics.topic: Radians: measuring angles by arc length
topics.notes: The definition (one radian gives an arc as long as the radius; 2π radians in a full turn) is universal and explainable without drawing the circle. Payoff: calculus results like d/dx sin x = cos x only hold in radians.

topics.subject: Math
topics.topic: What standard deviation actually tells you
topics.notes: The idea (roughly, the typical distance from the mean) is universal. Population vs. sample formulas (n vs. n - 1) get different emphasis across boards -- explain the concept and don't commit to one formula.

topics.subject: Math
topics.topic: Why 0.999... equals exactly 1
topics.notes: Settled fact that reliably surprises people -- strong hook. The 1/3 = 0.333... argument and the 'no number fits between them' argument both work. Present it as exact equality, never as 'close enough' or rounding.

topics.subject: Math
topics.topic: What the imaginary number i actually is
topics.notes: Definitional (i^2 = -1) and universal wherever complex numbers are taught; not every syllabus reaches it, which is depth rather than disagreement. Stay algebraic -- the Argand diagram is a diagram, so leave it out.

topics.subject: Math
topics.topic: Why dividing by zero is undefined, not infinity
topics.notes: Pure math identity, zero curriculum disagreement, and a genuinely common point of confusion -- good hook value.

topics.subject: Math
topics.topic: The difference between correlation and causation
topics.notes: Statistics fundamental: two things rising together doesn't mean one causes the other (a third factor, chance, or reverse direction). No diagram needed -- invented, everyday examples only (e.g. ice-cream sales and sunburn both rise in summer).

topics.subject: Math
topics.topic: The Pythagorean theorem, and why it only works on right triangles
topics.notes: Universal, ancient, undisputed. Purely numerical, no figure: a right-angled triangle's longest side (the side opposite the right angle) is found from a^2 + b^2 = c^2; work 3-4-5 and one more triple. Right-angled triangles only -- no trigonometry and no three-dimensional Pythagoras. Area and volume are a separate deck.

topics.subject: Math
topics.topic: Why a negative times a negative is positive
topics.notes: Pure arithmetic identity, universal. Explain it through the pattern in a descending times-table (3 x -2, 2 x -2, 1 x -2, ...) or the distributive law -- not a 'two wrongs make a right' mnemonic, which explains nothing.

topics.subject: Math
topics.topic: Why anything to the power of zero is 1
topics.notes: Follows directly from the index law a^m / a^n = a^(m-n) with m = n. Universal. 0^0 is genuinely convention-dependent -- mention it only to say it's excluded, don't try to settle it.

topics.subject: Math
topics.topic: Mean vs. median: when the average misleads
topics.notes: Universal statistics. Show skew with a small invented data set (one very large value among ordinary ones). Avoid real income or wealth statistics, which pull toward live economic/political framing.

topics.subject: Math
topics.topic: Exponential vs. linear growth: why doubling wins
topics.notes: Universal. Neutral examples only (rice on a chessboard; the thickness of a sheet folded in half repeatedly). Avoid pandemic or population examples, which drift into live-policy territory.

topics.subject: Math
topics.topic: Arithmetic vs. geometric sequences
topics.notes: Adding a constant vs. multiplying by one -- universal. Keep to recognising each type and its general term; notation (u_n vs. a_n) varies by board, so pick one and define it. At this level, recognise the pattern and find the next few terms. No series sums and no sigma notation. Exponential vs. linear growth is about which pattern pulls ahead over time, not about naming the sequence.

topics.subject: Math
topics.topic: Order of operations is a convention, not a law of nature
topics.notes: BODMAS, BIDMAS, and PEMDAS encode the same rules -- name all three so no one's board feels 'wrong'. Stay well away from viral '6 / 2(1+2)'-style puzzles: implied multiplication genuinely has no universal convention, which is exactly the contested territory this list excludes.

topics.subject: Computer Science
topics.topic: Why 0.1 + 0.2 isn't exactly 0.3 in most programming languages
topics.notes: Settled fact about binary floating point: 0.1 has no exact binary representation, just as 1/3 has none in decimal. Great hook. Say 'most languages' rather than naming one; no code.

topics.subject: Computer Science
topics.topic: Linear vs. binary search
topics.notes: Universal algorithms content. The dictionary analogy carries it; the payoff is that binary search needs sorted data. Steps in words or a short list -- no pseudocode, whose conventions differ by board.

topics.subject: Computer Science
topics.topic: Big O, without the maths anxiety
topics.notes: The idea (how the work grows as the input grows) is universal; formal Big O appears at different depths across courses. Keep to O(1), O(n), and O(n^2) with everyday analogies.

topics.subject: Computer Science
topics.topic: Recursion: why every recursive function needs a base case
topics.notes: Universal concept. A countdown or factorial described in words; the missing base case (infinite recursion) is the hook. No code or board-specific pseudocode.

topics.subject: Computer Science
topics.topic: Hashing vs. encryption
topics.notes: Universal and commonly confused: encryption is reversible with a key; hashing is one-way. Why passwords are stored as hashes is the payoff. Conceptual only -- no tools and no attack techniques.

topics.subject: Computer Science
topics.topic: Lossy vs. lossless compression
topics.notes: Universal. Everyday examples (photos and music vs. zip files and text). Conceptual; run-length encoding is fine as a simple lossless illustration.

topics.subject: Computer Science
topics.topic: Why computers count in binary
topics.notes: Universal: two stable states map cleanly onto electronics. A couple of conversions (1011 = 11) fit in math blocks. The slide format has no code blocks -- never include code.

topics.subject: Computer Science
topics.topic: Bits vs. bytes: why your download speed looks 8x smaller
topics.notes: Universal: 8 bits per byte; connection speeds are quoted in megabits, file sizes in megabytes. Give the 1000 vs. 1024 (kB vs. KiB) question one line at most -- conventions genuinely differ between courses.

topics.subject: Computer Science
topics.topic: Stacks vs. queues
topics.notes: Universal data structures (last in, first out vs. first in, first out). Everyday analogies (a stack of plates; a lunch queue) and one real use each (undo history; a print queue). No code.

topics.subject: Computer Science
topics.topic: RAM vs. storage
topics.notes: Universal (volatile working memory vs. persistent storage). The desk-vs-filing-cabinet analogy works. No current product specs or prices.

topics.subject: Computer Science
topics.topic: Syntax, runtime, and logic errors
topics.notes: Universal categories, though boards group runtime errors slightly differently -- keep the three-way split light. Examples in words, no code.

topics.subject: Computer Science
topics.topic: AND, OR, NOT, XOR in plain English
topics.notes: Universal Boolean logic. Truth tables fit as short lists; logic-gate symbols are diagrams, so leave them out. Operator notation varies by board -- use the words.

topics.subject: Economics
topics.topic: Opportunity cost, with a non-money example
topics.notes: Core micro concept taught identically across IB/AP/A-level econ. Deliberately avoid current policy examples -- use time/choice examples instead.

topics.subject: Economics
topics.topic: Supply and demand: what actually shifts a curve vs. moves along it
topics.notes: Classic misconception, taught as 'price change vs. non-price change' with no curve language: a change in a good's own price changes the quantity people buy; a change in anything else (income, tastes, the price of a substitute) changes how much they want at every price. Words and one everyday example only -- the curve version needs a graph, which slideshows don't carry. Mechanism only, no policy framing.

topics.subject: Economics
topics.topic: Comparative vs. absolute advantage
topics.notes: Universal core concept. Use two people splitting tasks (two students dividing a group project) rather than countries and trade policy, which drifts into live political territory. Invented round numbers only.

topics.subject: Economics
topics.topic: The sunk cost fallacy
topics.notes: Universal: money or time already spent and unrecoverable shouldn't drive future decisions. Related to the existing opportunity-cost deck but a different idea. Everyday examples (finishing a boring film because you paid for the ticket) -- no investing or business framing.

topics.subject: Economics
topics.topic: Externalities: costs and benefits that land on someone else
topics.notes: Universal. Small-scale neutral examples (a neighbour's loud music; a neighbour's beautiful garden). Avoid pollution and carbon-tax framing, which pulls straight into live policy debate.

topics.subject: Economics
topics.topic: Nominal vs. real: why a 'raise' can leave you worse off
topics.notes: Universal (adjusting for inflation). Invented round numbers only -- never real recent inflation rates, which date instantly and carry political charge. Frame the 'raise' as pocket money or a part-time wage to fit the audience.

topics.subject: Psychology
topics.topic: Classical conditioning (Pavlov), correctly distinguished from operant conditioning
topics.notes: Foundational, textbook-standard, zero live dispute about the mechanism itself. Avoid discussing the historical Little Albert study's ethics in depth -- name the concept, not the case study's controversy.

topics.subject: Psychology
topics.topic: The forgetting curve and why spaced repetition works
topics.notes: Directly ties to Memora's own Flashcards mechanism (spaced/adaptive review) -- a natural bridge from teaching a real concept to the product without an explicit pitch. Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve is well-established and undisputed at this level of description. How to lay that spacing out across a revision week is a study-skills deck. This one is the finding itself.

topics.subject: Psychology
topics.topic: Confirmation bias, with an everyday (non-political) example
topics.notes: Universal cognitive-bias concept. Explicitly use an everyday example (e.g. sports fandom, shopping decisions) rather than a political or social one to stay inside the no-live-controversy rule.

topics.subject: Psychology
topics.topic: The serial position effect: why you remember the start and the end
topics.notes: Robust memory finding (primacy and recency). Classic detail: about 30 seconds of a distracting task between the list and recall (e.g. counting backwards) wipes out the recency effect while primacy stays (Glanzer & Cunitz, 1966). A silent delay alone doesn't. Bridge to study habits (the middle of a long list or session is the weak spot) without overclaiming.

topics.subject: Psychology
topics.topic: Memory is a reconstruction, not a recording
topics.notes: Well-established (Bartlett, 1932; Loftus & Palmer, 1974 -- 'smashed' vs. 'hit'). Any quoted speed estimates from Loftus & Palmer must be verified in Stage 3; otherwise describe the effect without numbers. Keep eyewitness discussion general, no real criminal cases.

topics.subject: English / Literature
topics.topic: Denotation vs. connotation
topics.notes: Universal literary-analysis vocabulary distinction, no text-specific interpretation required, so no curriculum-specific reading-list dependency.

topics.subject: English / Literature
topics.topic: Dramatic, situational, and verbal irony
topics.notes: Universal definitions. Use invented, everyday examples only (no set texts -- the classic literary examples often hinge on deaths or violence, which doesn't suit this audience). Skip the 'is rain on your wedding day ironic?' debate -- contested and distracting.

topics.subject: English / Literature
topics.topic: A theme is a sentence, not a word
topics.notes: Universal analysis skill: 'love' is a topic; 'love makes people act against their own interests' is a theme. Invented examples; no set text needed.

topics.subject: English / Literature
topics.topic: The unreliable narrator
topics.notes: Universal concept. Use an invented narrator in a low-stakes everyday situation (e.g. someone retelling a match they lost, or a party they weren't invited to) and show the clues that the account is slanted. No set texts -- many of the famous examples involve violence or crime.

topics.subject: English / Literature
topics.topic: First person, third-person limited, and omniscient
topics.notes: Universal definitions. Rewriting one invented sentence three ways is the whole deck; second person can be a bonus mention.

topics.subject: English / Literature
topics.topic: The 'so what?' test: from spotting techniques to analysing them
topics.notes: Universal essay skill: naming a device earns little; explaining its effect is where analysis starts. Board-neutral -- don't quote any board's mark scheme or assessment objectives. A younger deck stops at building the paragraph (point, evidence, explain). This one starts where that stops: the effect.

topics.subject: English / Literature
topics.topic: Iambic pentameter, heard not memorised
topics.notes: Universal definition (five iambs: da-DUM x 5). Use a widely known Shakespeare line. Mark stress with capitals rather than board-specific scansion symbols.

topics.subject: English / Literature
topics.topic: Tone vs. mood
topics.notes: Universal distinction (the writer's attitude vs. the reader's feeling). Invented short example sentences rather than set texts, so no reading list is assumed.

topics.subject: English / Literature
topics.topic: Ethos, pathos, logos
topics.notes: Universal rhetoric vocabulary. Neutral persuasive examples (a school club poster, a product review) -- never political speeches or campaign material.

topics.subject: English / Literature
topics.topic: Active vs. passive voice (and when passive is right)
topics.notes: Universal grammar. The nuance is the hook: passive is the right call when the actor is unknown or irrelevant (lab reports). Don't present 'never use passive' as a rule.

topics.subject: English / Literature
topics.topic: Foreshadowing: planting what pays off later
topics.notes: Universal device; Chekhov's gun is the related principle. Invented short passages or long-established classics only -- no spoilers for recent books or films.

topics.subject: History
topics.topic: Long-term causes vs. short-term triggers
topics.notes: Universal causation skill. The assassination of Franz Ferdinand as the trigger of WWI, set against longer-term causes, is standard across curricula. Keep it to that structure and don't rank the causes -- historians genuinely debate their weight.

topics.subject: History
topics.topic: Why historians disagree about the same events
topics.notes: Universal skill: different sources, questions, and perspectives produce different interpretations. Keep it abstract or use a long-settled, non-political example -- never a live historical-political dispute.

topics.subject: History
topics.topic: Primary vs. secondary sources (and why 'primary' doesn't mean 'reliable')
topics.notes: Universal history skill; provenance (who made it, when, and why) is the real test. Neutral, uncontested examples (a medieval chronicle vs. a modern textbook) -- nothing tied to live political or national disputes. Whether an unreliable source can still be useful is an older deck. Here, define primary and secondary, and why 'primary' does not mean 'true'.

topics.subject: History
topics.topic: Why there's no year zero
topics.notes: Factual and universal: the count goes from 1 BC straight to AD 1 (BCE/CE use the same numbering -- name both neutrally). Fun hook: whether the millennium began in 2000 or 2001. Which century a year belongs to is a separate deck; this one is only the missing year between 1 BCE and 1 CE.

topics.subject: French
topics.topic: Passé composé vs. imparfait
topics.notes: Standard distinction taught across French courses (completed actions vs. ongoing, background, or habitual ones). Short invented example pairs; skip rare exceptions.

topics.subject: French
topics.topic: French false friends (faux amis)
topics.notes: Fun and universal: 'librairie' is a bookshop, 'actuellement' means currently, 'sensible' means sensitive, 'raisin' means grape. Stage 3 must verify every pair used. Leave out any false friend with an embarrassing or adult meaning.

topics.subject: Spanish
topics.topic: Ser vs. estar
topics.notes: Core Spanish distinction, taught everywhere. 'Permanent vs. temporary' is a known oversimplification (estar muerto is the classic counterexample) -- teach it as a starting point and show the well-known exceptions.

topics.subject: French
topics.topic: Tu vs. vous
topics.notes: Universal French usage (informal singular vs. formal or plural). Core rule plus a few everyday situations; regional nuances get one line at most.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.topic: Solids, liquids, and gases: the particle picture
topics.notes: Particle model at 13–15: in a solid the particles vibrate in place and stay close; in a liquid they move past each other; in a gas they are far apart and move fast. Melting and boiling give particles more energy so they move more -- the substance stays the same, and the particles themselves are not broken up. Do not mention covalent bonds or intermolecular forces; the older deck on boiling water owns that distinction. No particle diagram.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.topic: Elements, compounds, and mixtures
topics.notes: An element is one kind of atom (oxygen). A compound is different elements chemically joined in a fixed ratio (water is not 'a mixture of hydrogen and oxygen'). A mixture is substances together but not joined, so they can be separated physically (air). One sentence on atoms: protons decide the element. Isotopes, and what a chemical reaction rearranges, are separate decks.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.topic: What a reversible reaction actually is
topics.notes: Some reactions can run backwards: the products turn back into the reactants when the conditions change. The symbol is the equilibrium arrow, but do not explain equilibrium, equal rates, or Le Chatelier -- those are the two older decks. Burning wood is the contrast (not reversible in any practical sense). Melting and freezing are changes of state, not reversible reactions; the states-of-matter deck owns those.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.topic: A chemical reaction rearranges atoms
topics.notes: Reactants turn into new substances (products); the atoms are rearranged, not created or destroyed. Teach a word equation, not a balanced symbol equation: acid + alkali → salt + water is the neutralisation example. Don't name a particular indicator, and don't start redox or electron transfer (that's the older oxidation-states deck). Where the mass goes when wood burns is a separate deck.

topics.subject: Biology
topics.topic: The digestive system: each organ's job
topics.notes: Follow the path in words: mouth (chewing and saliva), oesophagus (the tube to the stomach), stomach (acid and churning), small intestine (most digestion and absorption), large intestine (water). Food does not pass through the liver or the pancreas; they add bile and enzymes to the small intestine. Name jobs, not a list of enzymes, and give no diet advice. What 'denature' means is a separate deck.

topics.subject: Biology
topics.topic: Food webs are not just long food chains
topics.notes: A food chain is one path (grass, rabbit, fox). A food web links several chains, so one species can eat more than one thing and be eaten by more than one predator. That's why a change doesn't stay in a single line. Use a generic invented web. No pyramid diagram and no conservation campaign. Why chains are short (energy lost at each step) is a separate deck.

topics.subject: Physics
topics.topic: Speed, distance, and time
topics.notes: Average speed is distance divided by time. One short example is enough, and the units have to match (metres with seconds, or kilometres with hours). This is a scalar rate: don't introduce velocity as a vector, acceleration, or the upper deck where kinetic energy depends on speed squared. Why heavy and light objects fall together is also a separate deck.

topics.subject: Physics
topics.topic: Series and parallel circuits, in words
topics.notes: Series is one loop: the current is the same all the way round, and the battery's voltage is shared between components. Parallel is two paths: each path gets the full voltage, and the current splits. Describe the loops in words -- no circuit diagram, and no resistance calculations. The deck about current not being used up is the single-loop misconception; don't repeat it as the whole lesson.

topics.subject: Earth science
topics.topic: The greenhouse effect is not the ozone layer
topics.notes: Two mechanisms students mix up. Greenhouse gases (including carbon dioxide, methane, and water vapour) absorb heat radiation leaving Earth's surface and send part of it back, so the surface is warmer than it would be with no atmosphere. The ozone layer is ozone high in the atmosphere absorbing ultraviolet from the Sun. Different gas, different height, different job. No policy, no targets, and no 'how much warming' numbers. Where carbon moves is the carbon-cycle deck.

topics.subject: Earth science
topics.topic: Why earthquakes cluster at plate edges
topics.notes: Earth's outer shell is broken into plates that move a few centimetres a year. Most earthquakes and volcanoes happen where plates meet: moving apart, pushing together, or sliding past. The pattern can be stated without a map -- at the edges, not in the middle of a plate. One line on the cause (heat inside the Earth drives the motion) and stop; don't pick a favourite convection diagram, and don't use a particular disaster as a case study.

topics.subject: Earth science
topics.topic: The carbon cycle: fast loops and slow stores
topics.notes: Carbon moves between the air, living things, the ocean, and rocks. Photosynthesis and respiration swap it quickly; limestone and fossil fuels hold it for millions of years; burning returns that slow store to the air quickly. Stores and timescales only -- no emissions policy and no 'whose carbon'. Where one tree's mass comes from, and what carbon dioxide does to heat, are separate decks. No cycle diagram.

topics.subject: Earth science
topics.topic: Relative dating vs. absolute dating
topics.notes: Relative dating puts rocks in order: in an undisturbed stack, the lower layer is older. That gives a sequence, not a number of years. Absolute dating uses unstable isotopes that decay at a known rate, so the proportion left gives an age. The half-life deck explains the decay itself; this one only contrasts order with a clock. No human-origins controversy and no disputed fossil.

topics.subject: Earth science
topics.topic: The water cycle
topics.notes: The same water moves: it evaporates, cools and condenses into clouds, falls as precipitation, then collects in rivers, lakes, and groundwater. Plants also release water vapour (transpiration) -- one sentence. It's a loop, not a one-way trip. No diagram. What melting and boiling mean for particles is the states-of-matter deck; what 'climate' means is the weather-vs-climate deck.

topics.subject: Earth science
topics.topic: The rock cycle, in words
topics.notes: Igneous rock forms when molten rock cools, underground or at the surface. Sedimentary rock forms when bits of rock settle and are compacted and cemented. Metamorphic rock forms when existing rock is changed by heat and pressure without fully melting. A rock can become a different type later. No diagram. Weathering and erosion (how rock breaks and is carried away) are the geography deck, not this one.

topics.subject: Earth science
topics.topic: Weather is not climate
topics.notes: Weather is what happens over a day or a week. Climate is the average pattern over many years (courses often use about 30). A cold week is weather, not a new climate. Definitions only: don't argue about whether the climate is changing and don't give policy. Why seasons happen (tilt) and how the greenhouse effect works are separate decks.

topics.subject: Math
topics.topic: Solving a linear equation: same move, both sides
topics.notes: An equation is a balance. Adding, subtracting, multiplying, or dividing is allowed if you do it to both sides. One example (2x + 3 = 11) carried to the end. Don't undo the steps with a different trick on each line. Order of operations is how you evaluate an expression, not how you solve; fractions-toward-algebra owns 'of'. No quadratics, inequalities, or simultaneous equations.

topics.subject: Math
topics.topic: Ratios and percentages
topics.notes: A ratio compares parts (2:3 means 2 for every 3). A percentage is a fraction out of 100, so 10% of 80 is 8, and increasing 80 by 10% lands on 88. One recipe-scaling example and one percentage example. No reverse percentages (finding the original amount) and no 'percentage points', which is a different idea from a percent change.

topics.subject: Math
topics.topic: Area and volume use different units
topics.notes: Area measures a surface, in square units; volume measures the space inside, in cubic units. They can't be added. Rectangle area is length times width; a box's volume is length times width times height -- which is why the units are squared or cubed. Stick to rectangles and boxes so nothing needs a picture. Pythagoras is about side lengths of a right triangle, not about area.

topics.subject: Math
topics.topic: From fractions to algebra
topics.notes: A fraction is a division. Equivalent fractions are the same amount (1/2 = 2/4). 'Three quarters of 20' means divide by 4, then multiply by 3. The bridge: 'three quarters of x' is the same move, written (3/4)x. Stop there. Solving for x is the linear-equations deck, and fractions with a variable in the denominator are a later course.

topics.subject: Math
topics.topic: Angles in a triangle and on a straight line
topics.notes: Purely numerical, no figure: angles on a straight line add to 180 degrees (e.g. 110 and ?), angles inside a triangle add to 180 degrees (e.g. 50, 60 and ?), a right angle is 90. One worked number example of each, no drawing. No circle theorems and no trigonometry. Pythagoras also uses a right angle, but it finds a side length; this deck only finds a missing angle.

topics.subject: English / Literature
topics.topic: Build a paragraph: point, evidence, explain
topics.notes: An analytical paragraph has three moves: a point that answers the question, a short quotation or detail as evidence, and an explanation of what that detail is doing. Courses nickname this PEE, PEEL, PEA, or PETAL -- teach the moves, and treat the acronym as a memory aid rather than the only correct shape. The usual failure is retelling the quote instead of explaining it. The older 'so what?' deck starts after this, at the effect on the reader. Invented sentences only, no set text.

topics.subject: English / Literature
topics.topic: What the beginning, middle, and end of an essay each do
topics.notes: Introduction: put the question in your own words and give a direct answer. Body: one idea per paragraph (the paragraph deck owns the inside of each one). Conclusion: answer the question again from what you showed, with no new evidence. Don't quote any board's mark scheme. Command words (what the verb in the question is asking) are a separate study-skills deck.

topics.subject: English / Literature
topics.topic: Simile, metaphor, and personification
topics.notes: A simile compares two things using 'like' or 'as' -- the test is simply whether it makes an explicit like/as comparison (a simile can even be literally true). A metaphor says one thing is the other; personification gives a non-human thing a human action -- for those two, the test is 'could this literally happen?' (it couldn't). Three invented sentences, no set text. Don't add allegory or pathetic fallacy -- courses don't agree on those labels.

topics.subject: History
topics.topic: Continuity and change, not just causes
topics.notes: Besides 'what caused this?', historians ask what changed and what stayed the same. Something can change in one way and continue in another: the printing press changed how texts spread, while copying by hand went on for a long time. Different from long-term causes vs. short-term triggers. Use a settled example like that one, not a live political period.

topics.subject: History
topics.topic: A source can be unreliable and still useful
topics.notes: Reliability asks whether you can trust the facts. Usefulness asks whether the source helps with this question. A ruler's speech can be poor evidence of what ordinary people ate and good evidence of what the ruler wanted people to think. Both judgments depend on the question. Primary vs. secondary is about when the source was made, not about these two tests. Neutral invented examples only.

topics.subject: History
topics.topic: How to read a century and a BCE date
topics.notes: For a year that isn't an exact hundred, the century is one more than the hundreds: 1865 is the 19th century, 1066 is the 11th. BCE dates count backwards, so 200 BCE is earlier than 100 BCE. Name BCE/CE and BC/AD once, as the same numbering. Whether a round year like 2000 falls in the old century or the new one is the 'no year zero' deck -- don't settle that hook here. No event from a contested conflict.

topics.subject: History
topics.topic: Facts and opinions inside a source
topics.notes: A fact can be checked against other evidence; an opinion is a judgment. One source often has both ('the harvest failed' vs. 'the governor was a coward'). Separating them is the whole lesson. Not the same as primary vs. secondary (when it was made) and not the older usefulness-vs-reliability split. One invented source, nothing tied to a live dispute.

topics.subject: Geography
topics.topic: Urbanisation is not the same as a city growing
topics.notes: Urban growth means a town or city getting bigger. Urbanisation means the percentage of a country's people who live in towns and cities going up. A city can grow while urbanisation stays flat, if the countryside grows just as fast. Definitions with invented numbers only -- no country rankings and no policy about where people ought to live.

topics.subject: Geography
topics.topic: Describing a population without a chart
topics.notes: A population can be described by the share who are children, working-age adults, and older people. A large share of children is a young population; a large share of older people is an ageing one. Births and deaths change that mix over time. Words only, invented shares, no real country and no policy about pensions or migration. Natural increase (births minus deaths) is a separate deck.

topics.subject: Geography
topics.topic: Natural increase is not the whole population change
topics.notes: Natural increase is the birth rate minus the death rate, and it can be negative. Total population change also counts people moving in and out. More births than deaths can still come with a shrinking population if enough people leave. Invented rates only. Don't use a real migration debate. The shape of the population (shares of each age) is a separate deck.

topics.subject: Geography
topics.topic: Site vs. situation: two reasons a town is there
topics.notes: Site is the ground under a settlement: flat, dry, near fresh water, or a hill that once helped defence. Situation is where it sits relative to other places: a river crossing on the road between two towns. A good site and a useful situation are different reasons. Generic or historical, not a modern city's politics.

topics.subject: Geography
topics.topic: Latitude and longitude, in words
topics.notes: Latitude is how far north or south of the equator, from 0 degrees at the equator to 90 at the poles. Longitude is how far east or west of the prime meridian (the line through Greenwich), from 0 to 180. Together they fix a position. Say that Greenwich is a convention, not a law of nature. No map. Why seasons happen is tilt, not this grid.

topics.subject: Geography
topics.topic: What a map scale is actually saying
topics.notes: '1 cm represents 1 km' means one centimetre on the map is one kilometre on the ground, which is the same statement as 1:100,000 because a kilometre is 100,000 centimetres. A larger scale (1:5,000 rather than 1:50,000) is a bigger fraction, so it shows a smaller area in more detail. The words 'large scale' and 'small scale' are the trap. No map needed.

topics.subject: Geography
topics.topic: Weathering vs. erosion
topics.notes: Weathering breaks rock in place (water freezing in cracks, plant roots, rainwater slowly dissolving some rock). Erosion is that broken material being carried away by water, ice, or wind. A river can do both, but the words aren't synonyms. The rock-cycle deck is the three rock types; this one is only break vs. carry. Don't turn chemical weathering into an acid-rain policy point.

topics.subject: Geography
topics.topic: Renewable vs. non-renewable resources
topics.notes: Renewable resources are replaced on a human timescale: sunlight, wind, flowing water, and wood if new trees are grown. Non-renewable resources are used far faster than they form: coal, oil, natural gas, and most metal ores. Definitions and examples only. Don't say what a country should use, and don't classify nuclear power -- courses disagree, and the definition doesn't need it. The carbon cycle's slow stores are a separate deck.

topics.subject: Spanish
topics.topic: Por vs. para
topics.notes: Both can translate as 'for', which is why they're mixed up. Para: purpose, destination, recipient, deadline (a gift for someone, leaving for Madrid, homework for Monday). Por: cause, exchange, duration, movement through (thanks for something, money for an item, for two hours, through the park). A few paired examples. These are the contrasts courses start with -- don't imply the two lists are the whole language. Ser vs. estar is a different choice (which verb, not which preposition).

topics.subject: French
topics.topic: French negation: ne ... pas
topics.notes: To negate a verb, ne goes before it and pas after: je ne parle pas. Before a vowel or a silent h, ne becomes n' (je n'aime pas, il n'habite pas ici). In everyday speech the ne is often dropped; say that once, and keep both parts in the written form this deck teaches. Don't work through ne ... jamais, ne ... rien, and ne ... personne. Tu vs. vous is a separate deck.

topics.subject: Spanish
topics.topic: Spanish adjectives have to agree
topics.notes: An adjective matches its noun in gender and number: casa blanca, libro blanco, casas blancas. Gender here is a grammar category of the noun, not a description of the object. Adjectives ending in -e often don't change for gender (verde) -- one example, then stop. Ser vs. estar is which verb to use; gustar is a different pattern. This deck is only the endings.

topics.subject: Spanish
topics.topic: Gustar works backwards
topics.notes: Gustar is not built like English 'to like'. The thing that is liked is the subject: me gusta el libro is closer to 'the book is pleasing to me'. More than one thing uses gustan (me gustan los libros). Stick to me, te, and le. Adjective agreement is a separate deck, and so is ser vs. estar.

topics.subject: Study skills
topics.topic: Plan a revision week
topics.notes: Spread subjects across the week so the same subject comes back after a gap, instead of giving each subject one long day. Start the topics you find hardest early enough that you can look at them a second time. The last session is recall of what you already studied, not a new topic. This is the calendar. An if-then plan for a single session, mixing problem types inside one session, and why spacing works (the forgetting curve) are three other decks. No sleep prescription -- sleep has its own deck.

topics.subject: Study skills
topics.topic: Why re-reading notes feels like studying but isn't (the fluency illusion)
topics.notes: The *why*, not the *how*: re-reading makes material feel familiar, and familiarity is easily mistaken for being able to recall it (a well-established metacognition finding). Stop at the diagnosis and one quick self-test (close the notes and try to explain it). Leave retrieval techniques to the active-recall deck.

topics.subject: Study skills
topics.topic: Active recall vs. passive review
topics.notes: The *how*: practical ways to switch from passive review (re-reading, highlighting) to retrieval (self-quizzing, flashcards, blurting, explaining from memory), and why retrieval strengthens memory (the testing effect). Don't re-explain why re-reading feels productive -- that's the fluency-illusion deck. Relevant to Flashcards/Quizzes without being a direct product pitch.

topics.subject: Study skills
topics.topic: Interleaving: mix up your practice problems
topics.notes: Well-supported (Rohrer & Taylor and follow-up studies), especially for maths problem types. The hook: it feels messier and harder, which is the point -- you learn to choose the right method, not just run it. Don't quote effect sizes.

topics.subject: Study skills
topics.topic: Ask 'why?' until it's obvious (elaborative interrogation)
topics.notes: Rated moderate utility in Dunlosky et al. (2013) -- present it as useful, not a silver bullet. Different from active recall: this connects facts to reasons rather than retrieving them.

topics.subject: Study skills
topics.topic: Teach it to learn it
topics.notes: Explaining material to someone else (even an imaginary student) exposes gaps -- supported by research on learning by teaching. Don't attach a celebrity name or origin story to the technique unless it's accurate.

topics.subject: Study skills
topics.topic: Concrete examples: making abstract ideas stick
topics.notes: One of the six evidence-based strategies the Learning Scientists summarise. The tip that makes it work: use several varied examples and pin down what they share -- a single example can mislead.

topics.subject: Study skills
topics.topic: Dual coding: pair words with visuals
topics.notes: Reasonably supported (Paivio's dual coding theory; one of the Learning Scientists' six strategies). Keep claims modest. The deck can't show visuals, so describe what to sketch (timelines, flow charts). Explicitly not 'learning styles' -- that has its own myth-busting deck.

topics.subject: Study skills
topics.topic: Try before you're taught (the pretesting effect)
topics.notes: Attempting questions before learning the material improves later learning even when the attempts are wrong (Richland, Kornell & Kao, 2009, and later work). Practical version: try the end-of-chapter questions first.

topics.subject: Study skills
topics.topic: Keep a mistake log
topics.notes: Grounded in the hypercorrection effect (confidently wrong answers, once corrected, are remembered especially well) plus retrieval practice. How-to: log the error and why it happened, then re-test it later.

topics.subject: Study skills
topics.topic: Worked examples first, then fade them out
topics.notes: Supported by cognitive-load research (the worked-example effect and fading). Best for maths and science procedures: study a full solution, then one with steps missing, then solve alone.

topics.subject: Study skills
topics.topic: Mnemonics: great for lists, useless for understanding
topics.notes: Acronyms and the method of loci are long-established for remembering ordered lists. The honest caveat is the lesson: they help recall, not comprehension. No mnemonics with crude or inappropriate wording.

topics.subject: Study skills
topics.topic: Command words: describe vs. explain vs. evaluate
topics.notes: Common across boards, but each board publishes its own official definitions -- describe the general difference and tell students to check their own board's list. Never quote one board's definitions as universal.

topics.subject: Study skills
topics.topic: Practise the way you'll be tested
topics.notes: Retrieval practice plus transfer-appropriate processing: timed, closed-book practice beats open-book review for exam prep. Board-neutral -- no specific paper formats or timings.

topics.subject: Study skills
topics.topic: Make it specific: 'if-then' study plans
topics.notes: Implementation intentions (Gollwitzer) are well-supported: 'after dinner I'll do ten equilibrium questions at my desk' beats 'study chemistry'. Practical and non-preachy.

topics.subject: Study skills
topics.topic: The hidden cost of switching tasks
topics.notes: Task-switching costs are well-established. Frame around notifications and hopping between subjects mid-session. Avoid the 'a phone on the desk drains your brain' claim -- replications of that study are mixed.

topics.subject: Study skills
topics.topic: Why sleep is part of studying
topics.notes: Sleep's role in memory consolidation is well-established. Keep it educational (why an all-nighter backfires for recall) -- no sleep-hour prescriptions, supplements, or health advice.

topics.subject: Study skills
topics.topic: Learning styles: the study myth that won't go away
topics.notes: Strong research consensus that matching teaching to a preferred 'visual/auditory/kinaesthetic' style doesn't improve learning (Pashler et al., 2008). Be respectful -- many students were taught it; frame as 'what the research found', not 'your teacher was wrong'. Point to what does work (dual coding, retrieval).

topics.subject: Study skills
topics.topic: Estimate before you calculate
topics.notes: A checking habit for maths and science: a quick order-of-magnitude estimate catches calculator slips and unit errors. Board-neutral.

topics.subject: Study skills
topics.topic: Spend exam time in proportion to marks
topics.notes: Practical exam technique: work out minutes per mark at the start and move on from stuck questions. Board-neutral -- no specific papers' timings or mark totals.
